questions.q: How is the motor effect best defined?
options: The action of a force experienced by a current-carrying conductor in an external magnetic field
The production of a current in a conductor that is moved through a magnetic field
The circular magnetic field produced around any current-carrying conductor
The turning effect on a magnet placed near a current-carrying conductor
questions.explanation: The textbook states it word for word: the motor effect is the action of a force experienced by a current-carrying conductor in an external magnetic field. The wire's own field interacts with the external field, and the conductor experiences a force. The second option describes the generator/induction effect, the reverse situation.

questions.q: In the equation F = BIl sin θ for the force on a current-carrying conductor, what does B represent and in what unit is it measured?
options: The current flowing in the conductor, measured in ampere (A)
The length of the conductor, measured in metres (m)
The strength of the magnetic field, measured in tesla (T)
The force on the conductor, measured in newtons (N)
questions.explanation: In F = BIl sin θ, F is measured in newtons (N), B is the strength of the magnetic field measured in tesla (T), I is the current measured in ampere (A), and l is the length of the conductor measured in metres (m). A tesla can be read off the equation as a newton per ampere per metre.

questions.q: For a straight conductor in a magnetic field, the angle θ is the angle between the conductor and the field. When is the force on the conductor a maximum, and when is it zero?
options: Maximum when the conductor is parallel to the field; zero when at right angles to the field
Maximum when the conductor is at right angles to the field; zero when parallel to the field
Maximum and zero at the same 45° angle to the field
Always the same magnitude regardless of the angle between conductor and field
questions.explanation: The force is at a maximum when the conductor is at right angles to the field (θ = 90°, sin 90° = 1) and is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field (θ = 0°, sin 0° = 0). The magnitude is proportional to the component of the field at right angles to the conductor. Students often guess the opposite — 'lined up must be biggest' — but it is exactly backwards.

questions.q: From memory, list the factors that affect the magnitude of the force on a straight current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, and state how the force depends on each.
keyPoints: The force is proportional to the strength of the external magnetic field, B.
The force is proportional to the magnitude of the current in the conductor, I.
The force is proportional to the length of the conductor in the field, l.
The force depends on the angle between the conductor and the field: maximum at right angles, zero when parallel, varying as sin θ. Together: F = BIl sin θ.
questions.explanation: If you recalled all four factors (B, I, l and the angle) and that three are simple direct proportions while the angle follows sin θ, grade yourself Good or Easy. They are all written straight into F = BIl sin θ.

questions.q: A conductor of length 8.0 cm carries a current of 30 mA in a magnetic field of strength 0.25 T. Calculate the magnitude of the force acting on it when the conductor is at right angles to the field.
questions.explanation: This is the textbook's Sample Problem 1(a). Convert to SI units first (cm to m, mA to A), then substitute into F = BIl sin θ. At right angles sin 90° = 1, giving the maximum force of 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ N.

questions.q: The force on a 10 cm wire carrying a current of 15 A, placed in a magnetic field perpendicular to the wire, has a maximum value of 3.5 N. What is the strength of the magnetic field?
questions.explanation: This is the textbook's 5.3 Exercise 1 Q2. 'Maximum' tells you the wire is perpendicular to the field, so sin θ = 1 and F = BIl. Rearrange to B = F/(Il) and convert 10 cm to 0.10 m before substituting, giving B ≈ 2.3 T.

questions.q: According to the textbook, who discovered the motor effect, and in what year?
options: James Clerk Maxwell, in 1865
Michael Faraday, in 1821
H. F. Lenz, in 1834
Hans Christian Oersted, in 1820
questions.explanation: The textbook records that the motor effect — the action of a force on a current-carrying conductor in an external magnetic field — was discovered in 1821 by Michael Faraday (1791–1867). For the exam the effect itself does not need a name attached; the mechanism does.

questions.q: From memory, give the 'two-field interaction' answer the HSC wants: how do two magnetic fields make a current-carrying wire experience a force?
keyPoints: The current-carrying conductor produces its own circular magnetic field (concentric circles around the wire, direction from the right-hand grip rule).
This field is superimposed on / interacts with the external uniform magnetic field, and the fields add as vectors.
On one side the fields reinforce to give a stronger combined field; on the other side they partially cancel to give a weaker combined field.
The conductor experiences a net force directed from the region of stronger combined field toward the region of weaker combined field.
questions.explanation: This is the mark-earning mechanism. Never answer 'explain why' with the formula F = BIl or with the right-hand rule — those are a calculation tool and a direction aid. If you hit all four beats (own field, interaction, strong/weak sides, net force strong to weak), grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: Use magnetic field interactions to explain why a current-carrying conductor experiences a force when placed in a uniform magnetic field. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The current-carrying conductor produces its own magnetic field — concentric circles around the wire, with direction given by the right-hand grip rule. This field is superimposed on the external uniform field. On one side of the conductor the two fields point the same way and reinforce, giving a stronger combined field; on the other side they oppose and partially cancel, giving a weaker combined field. The conductor therefore experiences a net force directed from the region of stronger field toward the region of weaker field.

criteria.descriptor: States the conductor produces its own (circular) magnetic field.
Describes the interaction/superposition producing a stronger combined field on one side and a weaker one on the other.
Concludes the net force is directed from the stronger-field region toward the weaker-field region.

questions.explanation: The marker is hunting for the interaction of two fields and the resulting asymmetry — not the formula. Writing 'a force acts because F = BIl' or 'because of the right-hand rule' earns almost nothing on this 'explain why' question.

questions.q: A question gives you the direction of electron flow in a wire and asks for the direction of the force using the right-hand push rule. What must you do first?
options: Apply the rule directly, pointing your thumb in the direction of electron flow
Reverse the electron-flow direction to get the conventional current, then point your thumb that way
Point your fingers in the direction of electron flow and your palm gives the current
Nothing — electron flow and conventional current point the same way
questions.explanation: The right-hand push rule is defined using conventional current — the direction positive charge would move — which is opposite to the way electrons actually drift. If a question hands you electron flow, you must flip it to get the conventional current before applying the rule, or your force comes out exactly backwards.
